newsitem.title: UK: British regulator homes in on fund mismanagement.
newsitem.headline: British regulator homes in on fund mismanagement.

text.p: British fund management watchdog IMRO, thrust into the limelight by two high profile cases in the last week, expects to see more significant disciplinary action before the year is out, said its chief executive Phillip Thorpe.

His comments came as British financial markets regulator, the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), on Tuesday published proposals aimed at making easier identification of those responsible when a company suffers catastrophic failure.

IMRO's (Investment Management Regulatory Organisation) Thorpe told Reuters on Tuesday that more disciplinary action has recently been authorised, but he said the watchdog had not launched any aggressive new campaign.
The organisation is also streamlining its investigative operations by bringing monitoring and enforcement teams closer.
"We have a raft of investigations running...There will, I'm sure, be further discipline coming through during the course of the year and some of it will be significant," he said.
Robert Fleming group was fined 700,000 pounds ($1.09 million) by IMRO on Thursday for rule breaches, after a five month investigation into dealing procedures at subsidiaries.
The action against Fleming included Hong Kong authorities securing voluntary compensation of nearly $20 million from a company jointly owned by Jardine Matheson and Fleming.
Last week also saw IMRO fine Save & Prosper Equity Plan Managers 115,000 pounds for breaches of rules relating to its personal equity plans (PEPs) invested directly in equities.

Then on Monday, the watchdog began a probe into possible irregularities at Morgan Grenfell, after the fund management arm of investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell suspended dealing in three high-profile European funds.
At the end of June, IMRO was conducting 51 investigations and three disciplinary actions were in progress. Some have been concluded but the total has increased, Thorpe said.

IMRO also is streamlining operations, to work more effectively. Thorpe said that within the last two weeks, it has restructured so that the separate monitoring and enforcement teams report now to the same director, Dan Waters.
"It's pretty much an efficiency change. What this will allow is an easier migration between monitoring and enforcement."
Headline grabbing is not the watchdog's style. The last week has been an aberration, with two major European investment banking organisations at the centre of IMRO action.
Thorpe said the timing of Fleming and Morgan Grenfell was coincidental. Fleming followed months of investigation, while Morgan Grenfell has only just come to IMRO's attention.

He said that much of the watchdog's time is spent working with the industry to ensure compliance. Last month, it started a pilot scheme, under which around 50 firms have taken the regulatory burden on themselves for 12 to 18 months.

Separately, the SFA, is trying to make it easier to identify those responsible in instances of catastrophic failure. Under the new proposals, the burden of proof falls on senior management rather than the regulator. The present regulations, although assigning ultimate responsibility to top executives, are thought too vague to be sufficiently effective.

The new rules include making "the senior nominated officer in each firm directly responsible and accountable for ensuring that not only are the control structures in place in the firm but that they are working effectively."
SFA chairman Nicholas Durlacher moved to justify the new rules, which are thought likely to stir up controversy.

"We do think that SFA should have the right to require senior executives formally to justify their conduct and competence in the event of a management failure which is so serious that it threatens the future of the firm." ($1=.6406 Pound)
